title: 10. Security & Auth: Encryption at Rest

objectives: What is envelope encryption and why is it the standard pattern for encryption at rest?
What is the difference between full-disk encryption and column-level encryption?
Why must the master key never leave the KMS?
How do you rotate encryption keys without re-encrypting all data?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Encryption at rest is the practice of encrypting data while it is stored on disk or other persistent media — database files, object storage, block-device snapshots, backups, logs — so that anyone with physical or administrative access to the storage (a stolen disk, an unauthenticated snapshot readout, a misplaced backup tape) cannot read the plaintext without the encryption key held by a separate key management service.

Encryption at rest exists because the assumption "the storage media is physically secure" stopped being true decades ago. Disks fail and get returned under warranty (still readable with forensic tools); cloud snapshots get copied between accounts by misconfiguration; backup tapes get lost in transit; SSDs retain data even after a "secure erase"; a malicious insider with database admin rights can `SELECT *` from any table. Encrypting the bytes on disk means that none of these failures expose plaintext — the attacker gets ciphertext that is computationally infeasible to decrypt without the key, and the key is held separately in a key management service (KMS) that can be rotated, audited, and revoked independently of the data. By 2024, encryption at rest is the default for every major storage system — AWS S3 enables it by default on new buckets, EBS volumes are encrypted by default in many accounts, MongoDB WiredTiger, PostgreSQL (via extensions), and Cassandra all support native encryption, and compliance regimes (HIPAA, PCI-DSS, GDPR, SOC 2) effectively require it.

The two main layers of encryption at rest are **full-disk/storage-level encryption** and **application/column-level encryption**. Full-disk encryption (Linux LUKS, BitLocker, FileVault, AWS EBS encryption, S3 SSE) encrypts every byte written to the device transparently: the operating system or storage service holds a data key, encrypts blocks as they are written, decrypts them as they are read, and the application above is unaware. This is cheap (modern CPUs have AES-NI hardware acceleration that makes AES-256 essentially free), simple (no application changes), and protects against physical media theft — but it does not protect against an attacker who compromises the running system, because the OS has the key in memory and can read the plaintext. Column-level or application-level encryption moves the encryption up to the application: the service encrypts specific sensitive fields (credit card number, SSN, health record) before writing them to the database, and decrypts them on read. This protects against database admin compromise (the DBA sees only ciphertext) and allows per-field key rotation, but is more expensive (per-field crypto cost, no indexes on encrypted columns, no range queries) and requires careful application design. The two layers compose: a mature system uses both — full-disk encryption for the broad defense, application-level encryption for the most sensitive fields.

The key insight that makes modern encryption-at-rest practical is **envelope encryption**. Naive approaches encrypt all data with a single master key — but rotating that master key then means re-encrypting every byte on disk, which is infeasible for petabytes of data. Envelope encryption solves this with two layers: a single **master key** (also called a customer master key, CMK, or KEK — key-encrypting key) lives in a KMS and never leaves it; for each write (or each file, or each database row), the service generates a random **data key**, encrypts the data with the data key, then encrypts the data key with the master key and stores the encrypted data key alongside the ciphertext. To decrypt, the service sends the encrypted data key to the KMS, the KMS decrypts it with the master key (the master key never leaves the KMS), returns the plaintext data key, and the service decrypts the data. Now rotating the master key is cheap: re-encrypt only the data keys (which are tiny — 32 bytes each) with the new master key, leave the bulk ciphertext untouched. AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HashiCorp Vault all implement envelope encryption as the standard pattern, and S3, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and most managed databases use it internally.

Real-world systems illustrate the patterns. AWS S3 server-side encryption (SSE-S3, SSE-KMS, SSE-C) offers three modes: SSE-S3 uses AWS-owned keys managed entirely by S3 (simplest, no customer key visibility); SSE-KMS uses a customer-managed key in AWS KMS with full audit trail via CloudTrail (every data-key use is logged); SSE-C lets the customer provide the key on each request (rare, used when the customer will not trust AWS with even the key handle). AWS EBS encryption encrypts the volume, the snapshots, and the in-flight data between the instance and EBS — all transparent to the OS, with a per-volume data key wrapped by a KMS master key. MongoDB WiredTiger encryption (enabled with `--enableEncryption`) uses envelope encryption with a master key in a KMIP server or local key file, and per-database data keys. PostgreSQL does not have native TDE (transparent data encryption) in the open-source build, but the `pgcrypto` extension provides column-level encryption, and EnterpriseDB and Cloud SQL provide TDE at the storage layer. The unifying principle: the master key never touches the disk, the data key is generated per-object and stored encrypted alongside the data, and the KMS is the single point of audit and control.

The trade-offs around key management are the heart of the topic. Where does the master key live? Options span from cloud-managed (AWS KMS, where AWS controls the HSM and you control the key policy) to customer-managed in a cloud HSM (AWS CloudHSM, where you control the HSM and AWS only provides physical security) to on-premises HSMs (Thales, Utimaco) for the highest assurance. Where does the data key live? Always alongside the data, encrypted — never separately, because separating them creates an availability dependency (if the key store is down, the data is unreadable). How do you rotate keys? Master keys: generate a new one, re-encrypt all data keys with it, retire the old (or keep it for legacy reads during transition). Data keys: typically not rotated per-object (too expensive); instead, set a policy that new writes use new data keys, and old data keys are rotated only when explicitly re-encrypted (e.g., during a migration). What happens if a key is compromised? Re-encrypt everything that key touched — which is why the master key is so carefully protected, and why envelope encryption is so valuable (re-encrypting data keys is cheap; re-encrypting petabytes of data is not).

The other big trade-off is performance and operability. AES-NI makes the symmetric crypto itself nearly free (~1-3% CPU overhead in practice), but the KMS call to unwrap a data key is not: it is a network round-trip (1-5 ms in-region), and if you do it per-record on every read, you add latency and you hammer the KMS (which has its own rate limits — AWS KMS is ~5,500 req/sec regionally for `Decrypt`). The standard mitigation is caching: cache the unwrapped data key in memory for a few minutes (the AWS Encryption SDK and DDatabase Encryption SDK both do this), accepting that a revoked master key takes a few minutes to take full effect. The other operability challenge is searchability: encrypted columns cannot be indexed, cannot be range-queried, and cannot be searched with `LIKE`. Workarounds include deterministic encryption (same plaintext encrypts to the same ciphertext, enabling equality search but leaking patterns), blind indexes (a separate HMAC column for equality search), and dedicated searchable encryption schemes (which are academic and rarely deployed). Most production systems accept that encrypted columns are write-only or fetch-by-id, and keep non-sensitive fields in plaintext for query flexibility.

Finally, encryption at rest is necessary but not sufficient. It protects against media theft and snapshot exfiltration, but it does not protect against an attacker who compromises the running application (the app has the data key in memory and can read plaintext), nor against an attacker with database credentials (if the database decrypts transparently, the DBA sees plaintext). The defense-in-depth stack is: encryption at rest (protects media), encryption in transit (protects network), per-field application encryption (protects against DBA compromise), IAM with least privilege (protects against misuse), audit logging (detects misuse), and tokenization or field-level encryption for the most sensitive fields (replaces a real credit card number with a token, so even the application rarely sees the real value). Encryption at rest is the floor — every system should have it — but it is only one layer of a mature data protection strategy.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Application: write record] --> B[Generate random data key DK]
    B --> C[Encrypt record with DK -> ciphertext]
    C --> D[Send DK to KMS for wrapping]
    D --> E[KMS encrypts DK with master key CMK]
    E --> F[KMS returns encrypted DK edk]
    F --> G[Store: ciphertext + edk on disk]
    G --> H[Discard plaintext DK from memory]

    I[Application: read record] --> J[Fetch ciphertext + edk from disk]
    J --> K[Cache hit for edk?]
    K -- Yes --> L[Use cached plaintext DK]
    K -- No --> M[Send edk to KMS for unwrap]
    M --> N[KMS decrypts edk with CMK -> DK]
    N --> O[KMS logs to CloudTrail + returns DK]
    O --> P[Cache DK for 5 min]
    P --> L
    L --> Q[Decrypt ciphertext -> plaintext]
    Q --> R[Return record to app]

    subgraph KMS Boundary
        E
        N
        CMK[(CMK never leaves KMS)]
    end
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
ENVELOPE ENCRYPTION
====================

write path:
+--------+   1. plaintext record     +-----------+
|  App   | ------------------------> | Service   |
+--------+                            +-----+-----+
                                            | 2. gen data key DK (random 32B)
                                            v
                                      +-----------+
                                      | DK plain  |
                                      +-----+-----+
                                            |
                              3a. encrypt   |   3b. wrap DK
                              record with   |      with CMK
                              DK            v
                                            v
+-----------------+                  +-----------+
| storage:        |<-----------------| KMS       |
|  ciphertext     |   edk (wrapped)  | CMK lives |
|  edk            |                  | only here |
+-----------------+                  +-----------+

read path:
storage -> edk -> KMS.unwrap(CMK) -> DK -> decrypt(ciphertext) -> plaintext
                                ^
                                +-- CloudTrail logs every unwrap

rotation of CMK:
  new_CMK -> re-wrap each edk (32 bytes) -> retire old CMK
  (ciphertext untouched: terabytes stay put)
```

### Walkthrough
1. The application calls the storage service to write a record; the service generates a fresh random 32-byte data key (DK) using a cryptographically secure RNG and uses it with AES-256-GCM to encrypt the record's plaintext bytes into ciphertext.
2. The service sends the plaintext DK to the KMS with a reference to the master key (CMK); the KMS encrypts the DK with the CMK inside its HSM-bound boundary and returns the encrypted data key (edk) — the CMK itself never leaves the KMS.
3. The service writes the ciphertext and the edk together to disk (or to S3, or to the database row), then erases the plaintext DK from memory; the on-disk artifact is `{ciphertext, edk, algorithm, key_id}`.
4. To read, the service fetches the ciphertext and edk from disk, checks its in-memory cache for the unwrapped DK (keyed by `edk`), and if absent, sends the edk to the KMS for unwrapping.
5. The KMS decrypts the edk with the CMK, logs the unwrap call to CloudTrail (or equivalent audit log) with the calling principal and key ID, and returns the plaintext DK; the service caches it for a few minutes and uses it to decrypt the ciphertext.
6. To rotate the master key, the operator creates a new CMK in the KMS, re-wraps each edk with the new CMK (a tiny operation per object — 32 bytes), updates the stored edk, and retires the old CMK; the bulk ciphertext is never re-encrypted, so rotation completes in minutes even for petabytes of data.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
# Mock envelope encryption: KMS holds the master key (CMK),
# data is encrypted with per-object data keys (DK) wrapped by the CMK.
# Illustrative only — use AWS Encryption SDK / Tink in production.
import os, json, hashlib, hmac
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

# Mock KMS: holds CMKs; never exposes them; wraps/unwrap data keys.
class KMS:
    def __init__(self):
        self.cmks = {}                       # key_id -> 32-byte master key
        self.audit = []                      # log of every wrap/unwrap

    def create_cmk(self, key_id: str):
        self.cmks[key_id] = os.urandom(32)
        return key_id

    def rotate_cmk(self, key_id: str):
        self.cmks[key_id] = os.urandom(32)   # NOTE: must re-wrap edks after

    def wrap(self, key_id: str, dk: bytes) -> dict:
        cmk = self.cmks[key_id]
        kek = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None,
                   info=b"wrap").derive(cmk)
        nonce = os.urandom(12)
        edk = AESGCM(kek).encrypt(nonce, dk, associated_data=key_id.encode())
        self.audit.append(("wrap", key_id))
        return {"key_id": key_id, "nonce": nonce, "edk": edk}

    def unwrap(self, edk_obj: dict) -> bytes:
        cmk = self.cmks[edk_obj["key_id"]]
        kek = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32, salt=None,
                   info=b"wrap").derive(cmk)
        dk = AESGCM(kek).decrypt(edk_obj["nonce"], edk_obj["edk"],
                                 edk_obj["key_id"].encode())
        self.audit.append(("unwrap", edk_obj["key_id"]))
        return dk

# Storage service using envelope encryption.
class EncryptedStore:
    def __init__(self, kms: KMS, cmk_id: str):
        self.kms = kms
        self.cmk_id = cmk_id
        self.cache = {}                      # edk-hash -> plaintext DK (5m TTL)

    def put(self, key: str, plaintext: bytes) -> dict:
        dk = os.urandom(32)                  # data key per object
        nonce = os.urandom(12)
        ciphertext = AESGCM(dk).encrypt(nonce, plaintext, key.encode())
        edk = self.kms.wrap(self.cmk_id, dk)
        return {"ciphertext": ciphertext, "nonce": nonce,
                "edk": edk, "aad": key}

    def get(self, obj: dict) -> bytes:
        cache_key = hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(obj["edk"],
                                  sort_keys=True).encode()).hexdigest()
        dk = self.cache.get(cache_key)
        if dk is None:
            dk = self.kms.unwrap(obj["edk"])  # KMS call (audit-logged)
            self.cache[cache_key] = dk         # cache 5 min in prod
        return AESGCM(dk).decrypt(obj["nonce"], obj["ciphertext"],
                                  obj["aad"].encode())

if __name__ == "__main__":
    kms = KMS(); kms.create_cmk("cmk-prod-1")
    store = EncryptedStore(kms, "cmk-prod-1")
    obj = store.put("user:42", b"ssn=000-00-0000, balance=1000")
    print("on-disk ciphertext (hex):", obj["ciphertext"][:16].hex(), "...")
    print("decrypted:", store.get(obj))
    print("KMS audit log:", kms.audit)
```

quiz.explanation: AES-NI is a set of CPU instructions introduced by Intel in 2010 (and AMD shortly after) that perform AES rounds in hardware rather than software. Before AES-NI, software AES-256 cost roughly 100-200 cycles per byte, which at modern CPU speeds meant encryption throughput of ~1-2 GB/s per core — a meaningful overhead for storage-heavy workloads.
